newsitem.title: CHINA: Gore to reassure China, pave way for Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Gore to reassure China, pave way for Clinton.

text.p: U.S. Vice President Al Gore arrives in China this week with a mission to reassure his hosts that a political funding flap and concerns over the future of Hong Kong will not harm a growing Sino-U.S. rapprochement.
Gore will be the highest-ranking U.S. official to visit Beijing in eight years when he flies into the Chinese capital on Monday at the start of a five-day trip.

His tour is the culmination of intense efforts by both sides to restore cross-Pacific relations after rows that sent ties into a tailspin, as well as to move forward decisively from the bitterness that followed Beijing's 1989 crackdown on student demonstrators in Tiananmen Square.
Chief among Gore's goals will be to reassure Beijing that the Clinton administration is committed to improving ties despite misgivings in the U.S. Congress, diplomats said.

"The U.S. has renewed interest in the relationship and the Chinese are welcoming this, but they're also a bit nervous with the financial scandal and things like that," said one Western diplomat in Beijing.

The Washington Post said this month that the Federal Bureau of Investigation had warned six members of Congress last year that they had been targeted by China to receive illegal campaign donations from foreign firms.
"(The Chinese) will probably continue to be nervous about the Congress' potential to mess up this relationship, especially given what's happened the last few weeks," the diplomat said.

The U.S. House of Representatives also this month approved a bill calling on Beijing to honour its promises on Hong Kong after the British colony returns to Chinese rule on July 1 in a move that has irked China's communist rulers.

Beijing maintains it has neither the money nor the interest to fund U.S. politicians and dismisses criticism of its plan to scrap Hong Kong's elected legislature after the handover as interference in its internal affairs.
"Probably his marching orders are to reassure the Chinese about the relationship," the diplomat said, adding that Gore would likely raise thorny topics such as human rights only quietly.

Chinese analysts said trade issues such as Beijing's growing trade surplus with the United States, its bid for accession to the World Trade Organisation and renewal of its favourable trading status with Washington would be on the table.

"They want to resolve some trade problems. I think there will be some progess on the trade surplus issue but it cannot be resolved at once," said Niu Jun, an American affairs specialist with the influential Chinese Academy of Social Sciences.

Gore's meetings in the Chinese capital are also intended to pave the way for an exchange of presidential visits that would be the first since President George Bush came to China in early 1989. But the new disputes are potential obstacles, Niu said.

Gore will follow such visitors as U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright in February and her predecessor Warren Christopher last November. Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin have agreed to an exchange of summits beginning later this year.
"It's probably feel-good messages to the Chinese... to prepare the way for Clinton," the diplomat said of Gore's visit.

Gore's meetings with Chinese host Premier Li Peng and other officials would show that the two sides -- at loggerheads in the past over issues such as human rights and Taiwan -- could smooth out wrinkles in a rapprochement some analysts say will define the world's most important relationship in the 21st century.
"If Gore's visit is successful, it would indicate the two governments can control the development process of the relations between the two countries," Niu said.
